newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan liberalising satellite telecom before 2000.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan liberalising satellite telecom before 2000.

text.p: Taiwan will liberalise satellite communications before the end of 1999, yielding its state monopoly to private competition in satellite telephone systems and other business, officials said on Friday.
The Ministry of Transportation and Communications said it had submitted a proposed timetable and plan for the liberalisation to the cabinet for final approval.
"The latest plan will open the market to private interests in the mobile and fixed satellite communication business by December 1999," a ministry spokesman said by telephone.

Parliament's sweeping liberalisation of the domestic telecom market in January allowed individuals for the first time to own and operate satellite transmission equipment, but did not explicitly authorise their use for business.
The new regulations deal with such commercial uses, allowing companies to offer mobile satellite telephone and satellite data transmission services, officials said.

Briefcase-sized satellite telephones were used widely by U.S. soldiers and reporters during the Gulf War and Taiwan "satphone" maker Microelectronics sold over 200 of the devices during that period, a Microelectronics executive said.
"Currently only the military and a few government agencies can offer satellite telephone service, but commercial demand for the service is strong," the executive said by telephone.
Today's satphones send their signals to satellites operated by multinational co-operative Inmarsat and calls are billed through local telephone companies, he said.
The next generation of satphones will be hand-held devices relying on scores or even hundreds of satellites in low earth orbits.
Although Taiwan operate no satellites, the plan is seen as opening up new market opportunities by allowing local telecom firms to sell access on Inmarsat and other satellite systems.
London-based Inmarsat, also known as International Mobile Satellite, operates a system of six communications satellites used by more than 50,000 customers worldwide.
Taiwan's January telecom laws opened the long-closed market to the private sector, giving unprecedented access to foreign interests. The government aims to complete the liberalisation by July 2001.
Under the reform laws, foreign interests are allowed to own 20 percent of ventures offering basic telephone services, a limit designed to ensure local control of the industry.
Major new foreign entrants to the market, all allied with local partners, include Japan's Mitsubishi, U.S. giants Sprint and Air Touch Communications, Hong Kong Telecom and Singapore Telecom.
